issues.body:
Cloned from https://github.com/philsbln/ipv6-app-testing/issues/15 in repo migration 

From Michael Richardson's early review on -00:
> Maybe there are a few new sections needed for:
> 1. residential IoT
> 2. on-premise services and appliances.
> 2b.  a subset of this would include Enterprise IoT.
> 2c.  I think of routing/switching infrastructure as being the original IoT,
    or, maybe, "Things of Internet"... because how does your XYZ vendor
    routing platform call v4-home to validate licenses or update firmware
    when there is no v4?
> 3. Among the v6-only, but-not-v6-global, would include SNAC.
  Right now, this mechanism is focused on low-speed, challenged STUB
  Networks.   However, one interesting way to deploy a cluster of systems
  (could even be entirely virtual) to an Enterprise would be with a v6-only
  STUB network.

@philsbln partially addressed in https://github.com/philsbln/ipv6-app-testing/pull/17 in a very abstract way.
Do we want to address such scenarios explicitly or is it okay to just have an abstract enough definition including these scenarios?

comments.body:
```suggestion
Some applications and services may assume the existence and reachability of the IPv4 loopback addresses (127.0.0.0/8) when binding to a socket or for communicating with other services on the same host.
For example, a web server may explicitly listen on a 127.0.0.0/8 by default. 
For True IPv6-only scenarios, system administrators may choose to disable IPv4,
including loopback. In such cases, applications may fail to operate correctly. Applications expecting to bind to a IPv4 loopback address may fail to start when these addresses are unavailable
due to a bind failure.
Applications expecting these addresses to be available for inter-service communication will result in these services being unable to communicate properly.

Because of this, when testing applications for the True IPv6-only scenario, it is recommended to test the application in an environment without IPv4 on the loopback interface.
```

```suggestion
This example keeps the end-to-end tests for the browser edge (F1, F2), where the browser genuinely drives the flow, as well as for the F3/F6 data handling.
```

Acronyms are created for these components but then aren't used consistently, or at all (e.g., ALS and LPA), throughout the rest of the text. I'll make suggestions where possible, but don't want to risk botching the formatting on the component diagram or flow table.

```suggestion
- an Audit Log Service (ALS), internal to the backend, to which the BMS writes audit records of security-relevant business operations; each record includes the originating client's IP address and other request metadata; and
```

```suggestion
- an external Logistics Partner API (LPA), operated by a third party, that the BMS queries for stock levels and uses to issue shipping orders.
```


```suggestion

```


```suggestion
For every input, verify that the BMS parses the header correctly (F3) and that the ALS stores it.
```

```suggestion
Point the BMS at a controlled DNS recursor that can filter A or AAAA resource records to simulate IPv4-only and IPv6-only servers.
```

```suggestion
For example, the ALS's handling of that address value (storage, comparison, and rendering) must therefore be verified for all address families and representations, independent of the connectivity scenario used for the flow itself.
```

```suggestion
- F3 carries the originating client's address in the `Forwarded` {{?RFC7239}} header the LB adds when proxying to the BMS.
```

```suggestion
The IPv4-only browser scenario yields an IPv4 client address and the IPv6 browser scenarios yield an IPv6 GUA, and each must be carried unchanged into the `Forwarded` header on F3 and into the audit record on F6.
```
